title: Would Manchester by the Sea be eligible for an Oscar considering the diversity rules?

commenti.body: Would this apply to foreign films as well? Eg if Perfect Days were considered for Best Film - the predominant race in Japan being Japanese with no foreign actors in lead/material supporting roles, does that pass the Oscars test because they’re “Asian”? Applying a U.S. lens globally misses the mark but would be so Oscars/American/corporate D&I virtue signaling to do so.

I mean, are you or OP even reading the link they provided? 

A film can literally qualify and meet 2 of the 4 required standards from how it goes about the marketing and distribution process alone, even after the movie itself is made-in a foreign country or not.

Parasite would be an interesting one as well. It's not clear if the underrepresented group has to be from a US or Korean perspective. If it's the latter, then Parasite would fail that spectacularly in terms of race.

Although depending on the number of women involved behind the camera, it should be fine overall.

Yes, I read it. The distribution standards don’t make sense either. A Japanese movie can be 100% produced/distributed by Japanese men and pass this test. What does that do for Japanese women or traditionally underrepresented ethnicities with big populations like Korean, Chinese, etc. in Japan? Nothing. I don’t think you understood my comment

"Submitting a confidential Academy Inclusion Standards form (RAISE) and meeting TWO out of FOUR of the standards will be required in order for the film to be deemed eligible for Best Picture consideration:"

They don't have to meet the diversity requirements through casting. And if you read through that link you'll see that within each of the four categories not all of the requirements need to be met.

It's an *incredibly* low bar that a studio would have to actively go out of its way to avoid clearing. If those standards were in place when Manchester by the Sea was in contention then it *absolutely* would have been able to meet them because they'd have made sure of it during production. (The Academy gave a lengthy grace period to allow for studios to meet the standards)

>The main cast are white men, most secondary cast as well. No disabled people there so standard A would not be met. Not sure about the rest. 

That's why they have four standards, so filmmakers are free to disregard one of them, such as on-screen representation. This movie is edited by a woman and the music is by a woman, so that's standard B. So if the studio has internships and apprenticeships for underrepresented groups (which they should), for instance, that makes it eligible.

You literally asked if Perfect Days passes the Oscars test because all the actors are Asian. If you meant to question the efficacy of the Oscar standard in general, your very last sentence was the only thing that even began to scratch the surface of that topic. 

Not to mention your stance still makes no sense. Why would you expect the effects of their guidelines to be so all-powerful and retroactively help women in Japan who worked on the movie after the movie was already done being made? It's an American organization focusing on making change in the jurisdiction it has the most influence over.

>That's why they have four standards, so filmmakers are free to disregard one of them

Not even just one. They can completely disregard two because they only need to meet half of the 4

It is quite clear. There's a full list of races and ethnicities in the list. Parasite would meet the demand.

The goal of this is not to solve all problems of racial and ethnic equality in all movie industries in all countries. It's about trying to have more representation in the higher echelons of Hollywood.

The goal of this is not to solve all problems of racial and ethnic equality in all movie industries in all countries. It's about trying to have more representation in the higher echelons of Hollywood, which is what the Academy is about.
Exactly. It's not a hard bar to clear.

>At least **one** of the lead actors or significant supporting actors is from an **underrepresented** **racial or ethnic group i**n a specific country or territory of production.

My reading of that is that it would be considered from a Korean perspective.

Although from reading further down, it wouldn't matter as Best Picture nominees, who were also submitted to International, don't go through the same process.

Yes, but the casting is only one of four categories, two of which only need to be met. The cast could be 500 straight white men whacking each other off over Andrew Tate, and as people from historically underrepresented backgrounds were involved somewhere in production or down the line then it would be eligible.

God, the misunderstanding of these qualifications never ceases to amaze me.

There are 4 sets of qualifications that cover all aspects of filmmaking. Productions only need to meet 2 of these which cover every department and they are so incredibly easy to meet that almost every production would meet them without even trying.

Yes it would have, this seems like obvious bait. Two of four low bars in order to be considered eligible is not a serious hurdle for a professional production made with real money by a studio to clear. I love movies which are mostly about white men. Nearly all of them even 12 angry men would be able to clear these bars, even if they didn't meet onscreen diversity standards.

It’s a low bar: A film can achieve this standard by meeting the criteria in at least ONE of the following areas:

Manchester by the Sea probably easily makes it.

We just remember the white people in it.

This is the Oscars i.e. the american film academy, Parasite doesn't have underrepresented groups in Korea, Koreans are however an underrepresented group in western cinema, I truly cannot work out whether people are being deliberate with their misunderstanding here, Parasite shouldn't win Korean diversity awards, it does meet the oscars diversity standards.

By the specifics of what is said, Parasite does not feature an underrepresented racial or ethnic group by it's specific country or territory of production. 

It is diverse by American standards, but not by what is specifically said.
